Photograph: George Frey/AP Utah Utah death-row prisoner released after new DNA analysis of 1985 killing Douglas Carter, 71, who has spent more than four decades on death row, was released on bail until new trial begins Abené Clayton and agencies Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.12 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.29 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Utah man who has spent more than four decades on death row was released from jail after newly analyzed DNA evidence showed that he was not connected to a 1985 homicide. Douglas Stewart Carter, now 71, walked out of the Utah county jail late on Monday night after a judge ordered his release on bail. He will have to wear a GPS monitoring device until a new trial begins. In 1985, Carter was convicted of killing Eva Olesen, the aunt of a former Provo police chief. No physical evidence linked him to the crime scene. Instead, he was convicted based on the confession and the testimony of two witnesses who later recanted their story. Though Carter also signed a confession, he has maintained his innocence and said he was coerced into signing it. Tennessee to execute a woman for first time in 200 years after governor denies clemency Read more Carter was tried again for the killing in 1992 but was again found guilty and sentenced to death. The state supreme court ordered a new trial last year, citing misconduct by investigators. A DNA analysis received on 22 September excluded Carter as a possible match to blood found on a doorknob and genetic material recovered from the handle of a knife used to stab Olesen, who was also shot. Judge Derek Pullan said those results further undermined the case against Carter, but said a reasonable jury still could conclude that he killed Olesen. Carter’s attorney Neal Hamilton said he was glad his client was off death row but was troubled by the amount of time he spent incarcerated. “We are profoundly grateful to see Doug finally go home, but we are also heartbroken by the theft of his life,” Hamilton said in a statement to KSL , Salt Lake City’s NBC affiliate. “When Doug was arrested, he was a bright young man standing on the cusp of his future. He leaves custody a 71-year-old man hoping to enjoy what remains of the twilight years of his life.” Hamilton is also urging prosecutors to seek dismissal of an aggravated murder charge still pending against Carter. Pullan had scheduled a two-month retrial for 2027, but last week Utah county prosecutors withdrew a notice that they intended to seek the death penalty. Utah county prosecutor Erwin Petilos told the judge that reassessing Carter’s bail was “necessary and fair” as the state continues to look at the remaining evidence in the case. Theresa Olesen, a daughter-in-law of Eva Olesen, said during Monday’s bond hearing that her family had “serious concerns” about Carter’s release. “By golly, we were hoping for a concrete match,” Olesen said of the DNA analysis. “It doesn’t mean he wasn’t there. We just want justice for Eva. And if he had any part of it we want that to be known.” Explore more on these topics Utah Capital punishment US policing US crime news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.politico.eu/article/speed-up.text: Presented by EFPIA By DOMINIC GIANNINI with CLAUDIA CHIAPPA PRESENTED BY View in your browser or listen to audio Want to receive this newsletter straight to your inbox? Sign up here to receive the reporting and intel from the Gastein Health Forum. SNEAK PEEK — Health security dominated the penultimate day at the European Health Forum Gastein, with calls for Europe to be better prepared to protect health infrastructure. — Parliament’s environment committee backs an opinion on the Biotech Act supporting a one-year patent extension. Advertisement Advertisement — Europe’s response to the U.S. most-favored-nation policy was a hot topic at Gastein, with France’s new pharma deal stealing the spotlight. Welcome to Friday’s Morning Health Care! It’s been a big week at Gastein and it only cost attendees a bout of food poisoning, burnout and one unlucky Italian getting lost in the woods, spending the night by a waterfall before being rescued by helicopter . This year also bids farewell to Clemens Martin Auer, who hands over the Gastein presidency to Nick Fahy, director of the health and care research group at RAND Europe. Mark your calendars: Our weekly health care calendar lands in your inbox on Thursday. You can also go online to export and plan your week or suggest your own event . Get in touch : [email protected] , [email protected] . Follow us on X: @chiappa_claudia, @domgiannini_ DRIVING THE DAY GEAR UP: Europe needs to better prepare to protect health infrastructure, delegates heard, as health security dominated the penultimate day at the European Health Forum Gastein. Spread out: Petter Iversen, chair of NATO’s Committee of the Chiefs of Military Medical Services, said there were different ways Europe could protect health infrastructure, which continues to be under attack in Ukraine. “You can spread things out, use a larger geographical area and hide things,” he told Morning Health Care on the sidelines of the conference. Advertisement Advertisement Hiding hospitals: One option is to move hospitals into underground facilities to protect them from attacks, he said. “When we are building infrastructures in the future … we might have to think about dual use. If you’re building a parking cellar, maybe you should have enough power or electricity, and also water supplies, so you can actually build a kind of hospital in there.” Eastern Europe is already experiencing increasing threats from Russia, with drones and cyberattacks now frequent events, Iversen said. Countries closer to Russia had good plans in place, he said. “Situational awareness is sharper closer to the eastern flank,” he said. “You feel the pressure on a daily basis.” Where we’re vulnerable: European pharmaceuticals and production are also at risk since supply chains are dependent on countries like China, he said. “We need to prepare to reduce our dependencies from whom we will not want to be dependent upon if it comes to a major crisis.” Prepare for everything: The health care system needed to be resilient enough to withstand shocks, including those that went beyond war, like earthquakes, summer heatwaves or cyberattacks putting stress on the sector, said Jarno Habicht, the World Health Organization’s outgoing representative in Ukraine. “You might have more patients, but you might be also without electricity, so we need to be ready for the shocks,” he told Morning Health Care. Read more about what Iversen and Habicht said on health security and Ukraine here . POLITICAL ADVERTISEMENT Sponsor: European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA) The political advertisement is linked to the EU Biotech Act More information about political advertising here . EPSCO INFORMAL MEETING: Health ministers met in Dublin on Thursday where they discussed tobacco and nicotine pouches, the Biotech Act, medical devices reform and cardiovascular health. Advertisement Advertisement On tobacco: Health Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi said the Commission remained committed to publishing a comprehensive review of tobacco legislation, including on advertising rules, this year and that there will be a focus on nicotine addiction. “We are very well advanced in the preparation of the proposals,” he said in a press conference following Thursday’s meeting. We’re close: Forthcoming legislation would address vapes and heated tobacco products; their use being twice as high among young people than the broader population, Várhelyi said. It is important the tobacco products directive is revised to address nicotine addiction “so that we can deal with the cross-border element of this and create a genuinely harmonized system,” added Irish Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill who joined Várhelyi at the press conference. “Colleagues are concerned about the capacity of nicotine addictive companies to create new and novel ways of getting children addicted to nicotine,” she said. Presidential priorities: The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU is pushing for the Biotech Act and Medical Devices Regulation to be finalized as the Council works on its position (more on where this is up to in the Parliament later). “This is the moment to deliver this because this is the moment when long-term decisions are made in this sector,” Várhelyi said. “But for this to succeed, we can only achieve it if we have speed, if we have simplicity and if we have predictability.” POLITICAL ADVERTISEMENT Sponsor: European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA) The political advertisement is linked to the EU Biotech Act More information about political advertising here . FRENCH DEAL DOMINATES MFN TALKS: France’s new pharma agreement this week has shaken up the Gastein forum, seeping into nearly all conversations (whether on panels or by the coffee machine lines) on competitiveness, drug pricing and geopolitical relationships. Some are reeling from what they say was a very unexpected announcement, which throws into doubt what the rest of the bloc can do, while others see it as an inevitable evolution of U.S. pressure. Recap : France announced this week a new deal with the pharmaceutical sector on drug pricing, to provide “more clarity and predictability to pharmaceutical companies.” Stay united: Morning Health Care reported yesterday that patients, payers, EU lawmakers and capitals urged European countries not to seek individual agreements to counter the effects of the U.S. most-favored-nation policies, urging instead for a united Europe. During a panel on Europe’s upgraded pharmaceutical legislation, speakers reiterated the message Thursday. Morning Health Care contacted the French government for comment but did not get a response. Austria is on board : “As Europe… if we do not now see the need to act more [uniformly] and more together, I don't know when we should see it,” said Stefan Eichwalder, director of the health systems division at the Austrian health and social affairs ministry. It doesn’t mean not doing anything : “It would be dangerous not to act now, but then I think we need to find ways of working together,” he said. Eichwalder added that it was important that national deals — with industry or the U.S. — do “not weaken the position of the EU, and in the end, the position of any member state within the EU.” The bottom line : Countries should work together “no matter how difficult it is,” he said. “I don't see a solution for Europe to go 27 different different routes.” Think this through: Yannis Natsis, director of the European Social Insurance Platform, said countries should be asking themselves this question: If we were to accept paying higher prices, what can we get in return? “From a first reading of this agreement, France is committing to pay higher prices in return for what exactly? And what are companies committing to delivering in exchange for these higher prices?” The bigger picture : “Many narratives are going around. Narratives that are used by different sectors to serve specific interests,” Natsis said. “And in this case, this narrative is used to ask and demand higher prices. But again, the question is: if we were to pay these higher prices in Europe… what happens to the other countries? Because if France signs an agreement, if Germany signs an agreement, what about the rest of us?” Pushing back : Richard Bergström, vice president of European affairs at health data firm IQVIA and former chief of pharma lobby EFPIA, pushed back. “If you read the French deal… there’s a lot of wins for the governments as well,” he told panelists from the audience. “There are requirements on clinical trials, requirements on manufacturing in Europe, and most importantly, there is a gain at the end of life cycle.” It’s a “quite balanced deal,” he added. OVER IN BRITAIN: The U.K.-U.S. drug pricing deal — which is hailed by the Trump administration and industry as a blueprint for other European countries — is running up against some challenges, our colleague Caroline Hug writes in. Four pilots rolled out to try to meet U.S. demands to double medicines spending as a percentage of GDP by 2028 are currently falling short. Britain’s new Science Minister Chris McDonald has signaled the government is willing to try new ideas. Pilots ongoing: The government — with industry and the U.S. administration — launched the pilots running through September 2027, and the results will inform the next drug-pricing scheme. The line: “What’s really important here is that we start with what is the objective we want to achieve, rather than the means by which we want to achieve it,” McDonald told Morning Trade U.K. during a fringe event Tuesday at the Labour Party Conference. “I don’t mind trying things, and then if they don’t work, then learning from that and moving on and trying some other things.” New blood: McDonald replaces former Science Minister Patrick Vallance, who played a key role in the U.K.-U.S. pharma negotiations. One pharma industry figure told MTUK that McDonald “brings rare commercial instinct to the policy debate.” Deal mode: “It was quite hard to reach an agreement across the entirety of the industry [on pilots],” said Shaun Grady, AstraZeneca U.K. chairman, pointing to varying demands of some pharma companies versus big pharmas like GSK and AstraZeneca which “invest very significantly in the U.K.” He added that conversations are “now moving much more into a bilateral phase where each company will engage with the government.” APPROVED: Parliament’s environment committee has confirmed its position on the Biotech Act , with 53 in favor of adopting the opinion led by Nicolás Gonzalez Casares and 11 against. It supported keeping a 12-month extension of patents under certain conditions. Parliament’s legal committee also voted to keep the one-year extension in its opinion. Coming to the table: The co-leads on the Biotech Act — Vytenis Andriukaitis (S&D) in the health committee and Wouter Beke (EPP) in the industry committee — will meet in Strasbourg next week to try and find a compromise on the patent extensions they can bring back to shadow rapporteurs. Making progress: Andriukaitis told Morning Health Care on the sidelines of Gastein that political groups will likely have “more compromised solutions” on supplementary protection certificates, cross-border clinical trials and financing for the law by the end of October.” Read more about what he said here . Feedback: Shadow rapporteurs on the Biotech Act on Thursday submitted their feedback to the co-rapporteurs following a roundtable between MEPs, Commission officials and industry on Tuesday. Remember: Some MEPs weren’t happy at being offered a roundtable in lieu of an independent assessment on the supplementary protection certificate extension (SPCs) while some NGOs were also upset they didn’t get a seat at the table. Catch up on the controversy here . COMMITTEES BOOST PREPAREDNESS, CIVIL PROTECTION FUND : Lawmakers in the health and environment committee adopted their position on the EU’s next civil protection mechanism (UCPM), which now includes health emergency preparedness and response. Details : The compromise text boosts the budget of the mechanism from €10 billion to €12.42 billion, earmarking 40% of the funding for civil protection, 40% for health emergencies, and 20% for flexibility. The position was approved with 61 votes in favor, nine against and nine abstentions. It will now need to be put to a vote in Parliament. Sneaky global health reference: The adopted text includes several references to strengthening global health infrastructure. For example, it says that “strengthening cooperation … as well as the global health infrastructure and the World Health Organisation is essential to enhance the global ability to act.” There have been four more deaths from the West Nile virus in the Netherlands, the NL Times reports . Reuters has the details on Sanofi and Regeneron’s $8 billion partnership. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘The naive American president, with his inattention to detail, craving for flattery, and disturbing admiration for autocrats, was easily won over.’ Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/Reuters View image in fullscreen ‘The naive American president, with his inattention to detail, craving for flattery, and disturbing admiration for autocrats, was easily won over.’ Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/Reuters Opinion US foreign policy It’s easy to see through Trump’s Ukraine ploy Kenneth Roth In advance of the midterms, Trump is blaming Kyiv for high gas prices while making clear moves to support Russia Thu 29 Oct 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.47 EDT Share A s the US midterms approach, Donald Trump is abandoning Ukraine’s democracy in a desperate effort to deny responsibility for worsening inflation. Yet this past weekend’s dramatic elections in Brazil and Serbia show that voters can see through such subterfuge. There is nothing like a political party’s corrupt indifference to the plight of ordinary people to galvanize voter turnout. If US voters follow in the footsteps of their Brazilian and Serbian counterparts, a Democratic landslide is likely. If that happens, Democrats in Congress must act quickly to rein in Trump before he does more damage to the US’s economy and global stature. Any objective observer would see that Trump’s war of choice against Iran has inflated energy prices, because Iran predictably responded by restricting shipments in the strait of Hormuz, through which much of the Middle East’s oil and gas flows. But Trump, never one to admit error, needed a scapegoat. Enter Volodymyr Zelenskyy . While holding off Russian troops on the frontlines in the Donbas region of eastern Ukraine, Zelenskyy’s forces have been damaging the Russian economy by attacking its oil refineries. That has finally brought the war home to ordinary Russians in the form of long lines at gasoline stations. It has also disrupted oil production, putting pressure on a major source of revenue for Putin to fund his invasion. The Trump-Putin love story’s next chapter: selling out Ukraine | Sidney Blumenthal Read more Trump is trying to blame the inflationary surge in US gasoline and diesel prices on these attacks, even though their effect on the global market is small compared with the diminished flow through the strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, with Russia making only limited progress in eastern Ukraine despite losing hundreds of thousands of troops, Putin has taken, as is his wont, to attacking Ukrainian civilians. He has bombed their cities and attacked their energy infrastructure to deprive them of heat for their homes this coming winter. He seems to hope that a freezing populace will pressure Zelensky to capitulate. Yet many Ukrainians remain determined to defend their country’s democracy from Putin’s dictatorship. So Putin has turned to his ace-in-the-hole, Trump. The naive American president, with his inattention to detail, craving for flattery, and disturbing admiration for autocrats, was easily won over. Trump has now openly sided with Russia. He has authorized the purchase of diesel fuel from Russia, financing Putin’s attacks on Ukrainian cities. The gesture will not noticeably reduce market prices before the midterms, but it allows Trump to make a nod of acknowledgment toward the affordability crisis that he normally derides . He has waived new sanctions on Russia which had just been adopted by overwhelming congressional majorities in the name of the late senator Lindsey Graham, a purported friend of Trump whose devotion to Ukraine’s democracy Trump now betrays. The Trump administration suspended delivery of defensive missiles to Ukraine and early-warning intelligence of Russian attacks just as Putin was intensifying his bombing of Ukrainian cities, leaving civilian residents to their fate. And it reportedly greenlit a decision by Trump’s buddy Elon Musk to slow Starshield , the version of the Starlink satellite internet service that Ukraine’s military depends on for its drones to defend the frontline against a vastly larger Russian military. Finally, Trump called for an “energy ceasefire”, by which he effectively meant only an end to Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries (Ukraine has only one badly damaged refinery), not an end of Putin’s efforts to force Ukrainians to freeze this winter. Ukraine is attacking what are arguably legitimate military targets. Putin is committing war crimes . Yet Trump condemned only Ukraine’s attacks, not Russia’s. The Ukrainian government would have welcomed a real energy ceasefire but rejected this selective one. Trump claims his embrace of Putin is an effort to build a relationship with him so he will negotiate peace. But offering him enormous benefits in return for nothing won’t force him to the bargaining table. The former German chancellor Angela Merkel believed that tying Russia to Europe economically would preserve peace with Russia. Instead, Putin acquired the means to invade Ukraine. Trump’s amateur diplomats – Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – are hardly primed to do better. Witkoff embarrassingly dubbed Putin a “ humanitarian ” for releasing one elderly American held in prison on concocted charges while Putin kept up the indiscriminate attacks on Ukrainian cities. The envoys still seem to think that Putin aspires for only a chunk of Ukrainian territory rather than the destruction of Ukraine’s democracy. Donald Trump has sold out Ukraine. He makes appeaser Chamberlain look like a man of iron principle | Simon Tisdall Read more Trump hopes his blame-Ukraine campaign will prevent a Republican midterm debacle. It should only reinforce voter sentiment that Trump is indifferent to their plight, that he would rather deploy smoke and mirrors than alter his corrupt, self-serving reign. Will a Democratic midterm victory make a difference? The American presidency largely runs foreign policy, with little input from Congress. However, there are some things that the Democrats might do if they take the reins in January. I would begin with sanctions on Russia. The latest round of sanctions won overwhelming bipartisan support, yet the legislation contained the traditional national-interest waiver that Trump invoked to ignore them. The Democrats should re-enact the legislation without the waiver. They might even name the bill again after Graham. Outrage against Trump’s betrayal of Ukraine is widespread among congressional members of both parties in Washington. If the legislation can secure a veto-proof two-thirds majority, Trump would be stuck with it. That might also break his aura of being beyond restraint. A successful rectification of US policy toward Ukraine might be followed by bills that limit Trump’s tariff authority or curtail the funds he needs to keep fighting Iran – as he is considering doing after the midterms. There is nothing normal about the current Republican Congress’s abdication of its foreign policy role to Trump’s self-promoting priorities. Ukraine is on the frontline of the global defense of democracy. The American people see that. So does Congress. Trump may be oblivious, but under Democratic leadership, Congress should take matters into its own hands. Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch.
